catalog_quote: [p. 116] Additionally, I take the rise in the root mora of 2s-past forms to be due more to penultimate word stress than lexical tone. If there were a rule that insisted on some kind of higher tone (as may be the source of the penultimate/accented syllable rise in the 2s-past forms), then this rule might not apply where there existed already a high tone, as in the case of the 2s-future Rising forms. Thus, the presence of a floating high tone in the 2s-future Rising forms accounts for its flatness in two ways, by keeping the penultimate syllable from raising, and by keeping the final syllable from falling. Similar comments could be made about the 3s-future Rising forms. [p. 70] The forms in Figure 21 are preceded by a (2s) low pronoun, and the verbs themselves also begin low. The past form (on the left) is the basic low and level tone pattern, which rises at the end of the penultimate TBU of the verb, falling again on the final verb TBU. The initial TBU of the following adverb is higher than any of the preceding TBU's, showing it to be high in comparison to preceding lows.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (306 pp, text; the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'A Comparative Tone Analysis of Several Bantu D30 Languages (DR Congo)', Author Kent Rasmussen). Extracted p. 143 (printed p. 116, running head 'Ndaka 3.5.4 Discussion of initial tonal analysis of Ndaka verbs') with extracted text: the passage 'Additionally, I take the rise in the root mora of 2s-past forms to be due more to penultimate word stress than lexical tone. If there were a rule that insisted on some kind of higher tone (as may be the source of the penultimate/accented syllable rise in the 2s-past forms), then this rule might not apply where there existed already a high tone, as in the case of the 2s-future Rising form…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndaka is a tone language (H, L, with depressor-consonant effects; three verb-root tone classes). The author, from his own field recordings, treats the word as carrying penultimate stress: an otherwise all-Low verb shows a pitch rise on its penultimate (root) syllable and a fall on the final syllable, which he attributes to penultimate word stress/accent rather than to lexical tone. The statement is made in passing inside the tonal analysis, not in a dedicated prosody section, and no independent evidence for stress (duration, intensity) is given.
new_statements.exceptions: The penultimate rise is said not to surface where a (floating) high tone is already present, e.g. 2s-future and 3s-future forms of Rising-class verbs stay flat (p. 116).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('penultimate word stress'); observed on trisyllabic conjugated verbs elicited in a tone frame <pronoun | verb | adverb>, i.e. phrase-medial, not citation-final, so the rise is not simply utterance-final intonation. Whether nouns behave alike is not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Rasmussen's Ndaka data come from his own participatory orthography workshops at Nia-Nia (Mambasa territory, Ituri) in 2006, 2014 and 2016; this is Ndaka proper [ndk] = ndak1241, treated alongside its closest relative Mbo [zmw]. No dialect differentiation is made.

sources.note: Tone dissertation (own fieldwork, mostly Ndaka and Mbo). No prosody/stress section; sec. 2.4.3 gives segments only. In the Ndaka verb-tone analysis the author describes 2s-past verb forms as rising 'at the end of the penultimate TBU of the verb, falling again on the final verb TBU' (pp. 70, 76, 84) and on p. 116 attributes this rise to 'penultimate word stress' rather than lexical tone ('the penultimate/accented syllable rise'). Nothing else on stress (a full-text search for stress/accent).
